extracted.intended_audience: math enthusiasts, puzzle solvers, and readers interested in mathematical art (general audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing and recognizing k-fold rotationally symmetric planar curves given parametric/trigonometric (or complex-exponential) expressions, and for predicting visual features (symmetry degree, number of loops, complexity) from integer coefficients. Also covers artistic choices (colors) for rendered images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remainder rule for k-fold symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: For an object to have k-fold rotational symmetry the integer coefficients in the complex-exponential representation must satisfy congruence conditions: k must divide both (m - 1) and (1 - n). Equivalently, m ≡ 1 (mod k) and n ≡ 1 (mod k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive from the invariance requirement f(t + 2π/k) = e^{2π i/k} f(t). In practice this is observed as 'both numbers are 1 modulo k' for the examples shown. The same approach generalizes to other remainders (type-2, type-3 symmetries, etc.) by choosing coefficients with those remainders mod k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariance equation for k-fold symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The mathematical condition for k-fold symmetry of a parametric/complex-valued curve f(t) is f(t + 2π/k) = e^{2π i/k} · f(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this equality on the complex-exponential form of the curve (convert cos and sin terms to e^{iθ}) to obtain divisibility/congruence constraints on the integer frequency coefficients m and n.

rubrics_metrics.name: First parameter relates to degree of symmetry (intuitive observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the displayed examples the first integer shown next to each curve is one greater than the degree of rotational symmetry (i.e., first number = symmetry_degree + 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a useful quick heuristic for matching curves to parameter pairs in the puzzle examples, but the rigorous criterion is the modular congruence (m ≡ 1 mod k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of loops/turning points (m - n rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A curve with parameters (m, n) typically has m − n loops or turning points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This more precise counting method (credited to a reader) can be used to infer parameters from a counted number of loops: e.g., Curve B has 21 loops and sevenfold symmetry, giving parameters (8, −13) because 8 − (−13) = 21. It is said to work for curves with simple parameters like these.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude of second coefficient controls internal complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: The absolute value of the second integer coefficient correlates with the internal complexity (number of internal loops/looping behavior) of the curve: larger |n| produces more internal looping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare two curves with the same symmetry degree: the one with the larger |second_number| appears more internally complex. Use this as an observational heuristic when matching images to parameter pairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign of coefficient indicates rotation direction (backward vs forward)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sign of a frequency coefficient indicates the direction of rotation contributed by that term: negative coefficients represent backward rotation (opposite orientation) due to how sine/cosine components appear in x and y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the puzzle examples a negative sign (e.g., −14) was used because the x part is a sine term and the y part is reversed; in the complex-exponential form this appears as an e^{−i n t} term, i.e., rotation in the opposite direction. The sign matters to satisfy the modular/invariance condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use complex-exponential representation to analyze and construct curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine the x and y parametric parts into a complex-valued function f(t) (e.g., f(t) = e^{it} + (1/2) e^{m i t} + (i/3) e^{-n i t}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This unified complex form makes it straightforward to apply rotation invariance and to reason about remainders/modular relationships between frequency coefficients. Readers unfamiliar with complex exponentials can still use the clock-hand intuition, but the complex form yields the formal congruence conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of n-fold symmetry determined by chosen remainders
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the 'type one' symmetry (coefficients ≡ 1 mod k), other types (type two, type three, etc.) arise by choosing coefficients congruent to different remainders modulo k, producing different structured symmetries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment by changing the common remainder to generate families of k-fold symmetric curves with different visual types. Note that as coefficients get larger, simple predictive rules may need modification or supplementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic/color choices using z and z-bar and photographic sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: To create visually appealing colored rosettes, combine z and its complex conjugate z̄ with complex coefficients (a, b) chosen for artistic effect; sample colors from a natural object (e.g., a photograph of a rhododendron) to build a realistic color wheel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farris uses such tricks throughout his work: choose a and b for aesthetic effect and map color wheels from photographs to give mathematical creations a realistic and pleasing coloration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clock-hand intuition for explaining relative rotation counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Think of each term as a rotating vector (like clock hands) with rotation counts given by their integer coefficients; faster-rotating terms 'catch up' with slower ones a number of times equal to the difference in rotations, producing multiple alignments and symmetries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the hour/minute-hand analogy to see why e.g. coefficients 1, 6, and −14 produce 5-fold symmetry: the relative catches produce (6−1) and (14−1) relationships that, via the modular condition, yield k = 5. This is an accessible explanatory tool for general audiences.
